articles.title: Jailed for being poor, forgotten by slow courts in Nigeria, saved by strangers online
paragraphs: This post by Fatima Zahra Yahaya is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

In February 2025, a letter from a jailed man named Thomas Jonathan Biodun reached the public after some Nigerian Twitter influencers visited his prison to play a friendly football match with the inmates. Biodun was in jail over a debt of NGN 1,137,000 (USD 758). In the letter, he said he had asked for help online before, but someone had called him a scammer.

One of the influencers shared the letter on social media. Another influencer, Sir Dickson, who goes by the handle Wizarab10 on X, pushed it further, garnering over 2.5 million views in one post. In his post, Sir Dickson said, “ Nobody should be in prison over a debt. It is not a criminal offense. I have spoken to @egi_nupe [another X influencer and lawyer], and we will be taking it up. Imagine rotting in prison because you’re poor .” A public donation campaign followed, and within weeks, it had raised enough money to clear the debt.
Punch Newspapers reported that Biodun walked out of Apapa Kirikiri Correctional Center and thanked everyone who helped.
Biodun’s story has a happy ending. But it raises a hard question: Should a person’s freedom depend on the benevolence of internet strangers and how many people share a post?

In February 2026, the Nigerian Correctional Service said that most people in its custody were still waiting for trial. Many of them have not been found guilty of any crime but remain in pre-trial detention. While some of them cannot pay bail, others cannot pay court fines. In Nigeria, the crime of being poor can land you in a jail cell.

Waiting is not a small thing. While a case drags on, a person may lose their job, business, or place to live. A family can lose its breadwinner, which can derail a whole family — or even a whole community’s livelihoods.
Jonathan Biodun is not the only person who turned to the internet to seek support for injustice.

Quadri Alabi, 17, went viral in 2023 when he stood in front of former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s campaign convoy. He spent months in Kirikiri Prison over a robbery charge that his lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, called baseless. Effiong also said the police recorded him under the wrong age, meaning he was charged and sentenced as an adult. On April 17, 2025, he was freed. The same day, Effiong asked the public on X to help his family move to a safer home, because they were still getting threats. The International Center for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that more than NGN 3 million (over USD 21,965) was raised within two hours.

Emeka Nzeruike was arrested in 2015, when he was only 12 years old, over an alleged theft. He spent 10 years in prison waiting for trial. In July 2025, a lawyer named Alexander Nzeadi, who posts on X as @_youfoundalex, took up his case, and Emeka walked out of court .

The lawyer wrote that Emeka had been alone, afraid, and forgotten, with no trial and no lawyer. He then asked Nigerians to help Emeka heal, learn a skill, and start his life again now that he was finally free. The post was seen millions of times.

Look closely at these cases. Biodun, Alabi, and Nzeruike were helped because their stories reached the right people. A letter found the right hands. A lawyer or a kind stranger posted at the right time.
Biodun said he was first called a scammer. That shows how difficult it can be to be believed online.
But what about the person nobody posts about? Not every inmate has a famous friend, a lawyer, or a loud voice to advocate on their behalf. For them, it can feel like no one is watching.
This is the worry. If help comes only to the stories that go viral, then luck decides who goes home. A sad story with a clear photo may win hearts, while a quiet case may be missed.
Raising money to pay for inmates’ legal fees or fines is not new, and it is not only done online.

In 2023, The Conclave reported that public-spirited people and a group called Prisoners Rehabilitation and Welfare Action (PRAWA), a non-governmental organization (NGO), paid fines to free 37 inmates from Kuje and Suleja prisons. The Interior Minister at the time had urged Nigerians to pay the fines of some prisoners to ease crowding in prisons.
Kindness is good. But justice should not depend on luck or others’ generosity.

I do not believe we should stop being kind. I believe we should fix the courts, so that kindness is not the only hope a poor person has. If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home.
Social media is already doing one useful thing. It shows us real faces and real stories where the system is failing. Smart leaders, lawyers, and judges can listen, and they can fix it.
Until then, every shared post is a sign that Nigerians care. It is also a sign that the courts must do better. Everyone in Nigeria deserves a fair day in court.

articles.title: Doctors in Congress used to lean Republican – the 120th Congress marks a historic shift
paragraphs: The 120th Congress, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, will have 20 physicians as members, along with twice that number of members who have other professional health backgrounds.

This physician class will make history for including the most Democratic physicians in a single Congress – 11 – in American history – a marked shift from the Republican dominance of previous physician members. These Democratic physicians made their professional expertise and their health policy ideas centerpieces of their campaigns, and now they have the opportunity to advance their health policy agendas.

I am a political scientist who studies the partisan politics of health and health policy in the U.S. While physicians have long shaped American health policy, the physician class elected to the upcoming Congress is the most Democratic in the modern era.

The Democratic physician class in the Senate includes South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Andrews made reproductive health and rural healthcare access core tenets of her campaign. For instance, her campaign website stressed that “As a doctor and a mom, I’ve cared for women in some of the most difficult moments of their lives. … I’ll fight to: Restore the protections of Roe v. Wade, Guarantee access to contraception and infertility care, Expand maternal health services, especially in rural areas.”

In the House of Representatives, the Democratic physician class includes California’s Richard Pan, also a pediatrician. Pan’s campaign website, which featured many pictures and references to his physician background and stressed the importance of holding “RFK accountable for endangering Americans” – referring to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – as well as fighting to lower prescription drug costs, preventing the continued withering of the Affordable Care Act and banning prior authorization.

Other Democratic medical doctors who will be serving in the 120th Congress include two newly elected members in the House, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey and Amish Shah of Arizona, in addition to six returning representatives. Newly elected to the Senate alongside Andrews is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, an epidemiologist with a medical doctorate.

Beyond Congress, Democratic medical doctors will also serve as governors – with Amy Acton newly elected in Ohio and Josh Green reelected in Hawaii – as well as in numerous state legislative positions.

Physicians have played important roles in shaping American politics and health policies, back to the nation’s founding. For instance, Pennsylvania’s Dr. Benjamin Rush, an early public health advocate who led the city of Philadelphia through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793, was the only person with a medical degree to sign the Declaration of Independence.

Since the late 1980s, the number of physicians serving in Congress has increased substantially term over term. My colleagues and I have documented this rise, as well as how physician members of the House have influenced policy.

We found that physician members of the House were more active and effective in enacting health policy than other members. Physician members were more likely to sponsor health legislation, and their health bills advanced further in the legislative process. This was true for physicians from both parties, both on and off congressional health-related committees.

Since at least 1973, when our data begin, physician House members’ congressional voting behaviors and their health policies have been more conservative than other members on average, even those of their own parties. For example, we found that physician members were more likely to sponsor bills related to curbing abortion access, repealing the ACA and protecting private sector physician autonomy.

However, one of the most striking changes we observed was the shift from the Republican dominance of physician members of Congress to the steadily increasing number of Democratic physicians elected since 2015. That year, there were just two Democratic physicians in Congress, but the 119th Congress – 2025-2027 – has six Democratic physicians. The upcoming Congress will nearly double that amount, with the largest class of Democratic members with medical doctorates in American history.

It will be the first Democratic physician majority since 1995, during the 103rd Congress, when two out of the three physician House members were Democrats. Before 1995, physician members were much rarer, but the majority of them were Republicans. Between 1995 and 2023, 80% of physician members were Republicans.
These partisan changes reflect the broader partisan shifts within the medical community itself.

For most of the 20th century, the majority of physicians – both in Congress and more generally as a group – were Republicans. The American Medical Association was largely a conservative organization .
The party loyalties of today’s physician class mirror the slowly shifting demographics of physicians as a group.
Since the 1970s – and especially since the 1990s – medical school applicants and new physicians have become more diverse in terms of gender, race and ethnicity.

These groups tend to identify as Democrats at higher rates, though medicine as a field continues to be dominated by white men . Additionally, becoming a physician obviously requires getting an undergraduate and a professional degree, but higher educational attainment alone has also become increasingly related to Democratic support.
Beyond these more glacial demographic changes, three Trump-era events have shaped the political mobilization of Democratic physicians.

First, the partisan politics of COVID-19 and especially the politicization of the COVID-19 vaccine, has been associated with decreasing trust in medicine and science from Republican-aligned voters and an increase in physicians’ Democratic support.

Second, the elevation of Kennedy as HHS secretary, whose own vaccine skepticism has long run contrary to medical science and the advice of physicians, further pitted many physicians against the Republican Party .

Finally, the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned the Constitutional right to abortion, also appears to have politically mobilized many OB-GYNs and other women’s health professionals in response to threats to the care they provide and their professional livelihoods.
All these factors have contributed to a new physician class in Congress that is more Democratic and liberal in their health policy views than previous years.

Ultimately, what this difference means for future public policy remains to be seen. However, if politicians’ campaign priorities portend their legislative activity, there may be a more active push than Congress has ever seen for health reforms related to reproductive healthcare, rural health, prescription drug pricing, bans on prior authorization requirements by health insurers and maybe even Medicare for all .

articles.title: Sandagiin Byambatsogt
paragraphs: Sandagiin Byambatsogt (Mongolian: Сандагийн Бямбацогт; born 14 September 1974) is a Mongolian politician and public administration manager who has been the Chairman of the State Great Khural since 2026. He has served as a member of the State Great Khural since 2008, having been elected five times to the parliament. A member of the Mongolian People's Party (MPP), he has also served as Chief Cabinet Secretary from 2025 to 2026, Minister of Defense from 2024 to 2025, Minister of Road and Transport from 2022 to 2024, and Minister of Justice and Home Affairs from 2016 to 2017.

On 19 November 2026, incumbent President of Mongolia Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh was relieved of his duties. Consequently, as chairman of the State Great Khural, Byambatsogt assumed the presidency as acting officeholder until a new president is elected within four months.

Byambatsogt was born in Khovd City (also called Jargalant district), the provincial capital of Khovd Province, on 14 September 1974. He was born as the eldest of six siblings. At the age of six, his father, Sandag, died of health complications. Byambatsogt completed his secondary education at No.2 Secondary School in his hometown in 1992. Subsequently, he enrolled at the Military University (present-day National Defense University); though the exact information regarding his military service and time at the university remains unknown. In 1997, he pursued higher education in economics, earning a degree from the Finance and Economics Institute in 1999.

From 1998 to 2000, he was the Director General of "Hovdiin Urguu" Co. Ltd. He then became the Director of the "New Progress" company in 2000, a position he held until 2006. He furthered his studies at Maastricht University in the Netherlands, obtaining a master's degree in economics in 2005. His leadership at "New Progress" led to the formation of the "New Progress" Group, where he served as the Chair of the Board of Directors from 2006 to 2008 and later as its President in 2008. In 2014, he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Legal Studies from the School of Law at the National University of Mongolia.

In 2008, Byambatsogt was elected to the State Great Khural, representing the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party (MPRP) and the 16th constituency in Khovd Province. He was re-elected from Khovd in the 2012 parliamentary election. In 2013, he was elected as the leader of the MPP (renamed MPRP) minority caucus, guiding the legislative agenda of his party. He served in this position until 2016.

Byambatsogt secured another term as lawmaker in the 2016 parliamentary elections, during which the MPP secured 72 seats, enough for forming an all-MPP cabinet. In 2016, he was appointed Minister of Justice and Internal Affairs by Prime Minister Jargaltulgyn Erdenebat. His ministerial tenure was cut short when Erdenebat was dismissed by parliament in October 2017.

In 2018, he was made Chairman of the Standing Committee on State Structure, a position he held until 2020, when he was re-elected. From 2022 to 2024, he served as the Minister of Road and Transport Development of the cabinet led by Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene. During his tenure, he signed the Open Skies Agreement with the United States, aimed at improving air connectivity between the two nations, on 4 August 2023.

In July 2024, he secured his fifth consecutive legislative term from Khovd and was subsequently made Minister of Defense by re-appointed Prime Minister Oyun-Erdene. Following the collapse of the second Oyun-Erdene cabinet, Byambatsogt continued to serve as government minister when he was renominated as Chief Cabinet Secretary by succeeding Prime Minister Gombojavyn Zandanshatar on 17 June 2025.

He was appointed (84–20) as Chairman of the State Great Khural by the legislature on 3 April 2026 following the resignation of Zandanshatar and nomination of MPP chair and outgoing speaker Nyam-Osoryn Uchral as premier. The "Open Parliament" initiative (Нээлттэй парламент), an online transparency reform and modernization of the parliamentary electronic platform, was commenced during Byambatsogt's tenure. The policy, aiming to improve public access to information, expanded the transparency of all lawmaker's attendence, legislative reports, and bill proposals.

On 19 November 2026, Byambatsogt assumed the presidential office as speaker following the voluntary resignation of sitting President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh. He is serving as the acting president until the next presidential elections are held by March 2027.

Prior to Khürelsükh's resignation, the media speculated that Byambatsogt is one of the potential presidential candidates of the MPP. However, on 20 November 2026, he told the media that he will not run in the elections and remains committed to his stance.

Byambatsogt is married with three children, the youngest two being twins. He is fluent in English.

Byambatsogt has been an avid fan and player of volleyball since his childhood. With a first-class qualification in volleyball, he has promoted the sport in his home province during his legislative tenure. In 2014, he became the best male volleyball player during the annual "State Great Khural Cup," where public officials from various state institutions compete in. He is a founder and supporter of the "Altain Bars" Volleyball Club, a volleyball team based in Khovd.
Alongside volleyball, he is also an accomplished mountaineer. He has climbed several peaks in western Mongolia, notably Altai Tavan Bogd, Tsambagarav, and Mönkhkhairkhan Mountain.

articles.title: Putin hopes hardship will force Ukrainians to sue for peace – polling suggests it won’t work
paragraphs: Vladimir Putin has a theory of victory in Ukraine.

It’s not the Russian president’s first theory – that was a quick, dayslong campaign – nor his second or third, which involved different land offensives in the east that quickly petered out. Instead, Putin’s latest hypothesis is that the relentless bombing of Ukrainian cities will impose so much hardship on civilians that they will concede to Russia’s war aims.

Yet, as experts on conflict and public opinion, we believe there is a significant problem with this idea. Chiefly, extensive academic research shows that airpower alone rarely achieves decisive political goals.

Bombs terrorize civilians, but our survey findings in Ukraine suggest they don’t change war outcome preferences. Indeed, recent data shows that suffering from power outages and wartime stress in Ukraine has no relationship to support for territorial concessions to Putin.
The targeting of Ukraine infrastructure has been part of Russia’s way of war since the invasion of February 2022.

But since August 2026, Russia has significantly stepped up its attacks against Ukrainian power plants and grid systems, especially in Kyiv. And due to Ukrainian air defense shortages, more of Moscow’s missiles and jet-powered drones are finding their targets.
Russia aims to degrade the quality of life of Ukrainians, depriving them of electricity, water and transportation, according to a recently intercepted Russian military document .

“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, adding: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.”
The broader Russian aim appears to be to make the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable, imposing so much hardship that residents will either depart or revolt against continued war.
In combination with more aggressive Russian tactics and hard-right Ukraine skepticism in Europe, Putin calculates Ukraine will eventually be broken, isolated and defeated.

The city destruction strategy is not a new method of warfare by the Russian state. Post-Soviet Russia first employed a version of it during the first Chechen war of the mid 1990s, when much of the city of Grozny was reduced to rubble . The strategy was later revived by Russian airplanes in Aleppo, Syria .

But is there any evidence for Putin’s theory of victory? Polling suggests not. Along with the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, we polled a nationally representative sample of 1,801 Ukrainians from June 9-26, 2026.

The survey used a computer-aided telephone questionnaire and the results shown were proportionately weighted to accurately portray the view of residents in the area controlled by the Ukrainian government in Kyiv. It was the latest in a series of such nationwide polls we have conducted since December 2019.

There is no question that the Ukrainian population has been deeply traumatized by the escalation of the war since 2022. We asked Ukrainians nine well-being questions, which enabled us to create a stress index computed from how often they have experienced psychological symptoms since February 2022.

The results on the index reveal that nearly 1 in 4 Ukrainians suffer from high levels of stress characterized by concentration problems, depression, irritability, distrust, physical weakness and other physical problems. More than 40% of the respondents in the latest survey indicated that they experienced two indicators of stress – nervousness and anxiety – often or nearly always.

Stress is also related to war exposures. Asked about experiences of violence, roughly 20% of respondents said that they or a family member were personally injured due to Russian attacks, and 20% have directly witnessed violence by Russian forces. Sixty-nine percent of Ukrainians have a family member or close friend who has died as a result of this war.

Power outages have been rampant across the country over the past year, disrupting everyday life. Overall, 65% of Ukrainians reported losing utilities “often” or “very often.” Only 1.4% of Ukrainians report having never lost power since 2022, and just 9% say they rarely lost power.

There are important regional differences, however. While 73% of residents in Kyiv report that they lost power “often” or “very often,” the corresponding figure for residents in the western region is 54%.

While levels of stress are highly correlated with experiences of violence and a frequent loss of utilities, we examined whether this cumulative hardship affects preferences for a ceasefire. The survey asked whether the current front line should be accepted as a ceasefire line for the sake of peace.
The Ukrainian government has said it is willing to accept this position, but it remains controversial as it concedes part of the country’s territory to Russia, even if only temporarily.

Zelenskyy announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that freezing the current line of fighting was an option for negotiating peace; the Russian government, for its part, still covets all of the Donbas region of Ukraine and more.

Ukrainians are highly divided on accepting the current front line, with 39% of respondents in our latest survey indicating they would – with varying degrees of reluctance – be open to that possibility, compared to 38% who would not.

Critically, experiencing violence first-hand appears not to shape Ukrainian willingness to tolerate the de facto partition of their country at the current front line. Further, neither those who are more stressed nor those who have experienced more frequent power outages are more likely to favor accepting the existing front line as a ceasefire line.

Our polling data from summer 2026 is affirmed by more recent polling by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology that supports the argument that bombing will not make Ukrainians more accepting of conceding territory.

In a survey fielded from Oct. 6-18, 61% of Ukrainians rejected giving Russia full control of the Donbas region in return for a ceasefire and security guarantees. Indeed, the institute has asked this question in seven polls throughout 2026, and opposition to conceding Donbas has risen from 54% in January to 61% over the course of the year. Kyiv has been pummeled by Russian missiles and drones in recent weeks. But among all Ukrainian regions surveyed, Kyiv respondents had the lowest support for conceding the Donbas territory.

Another question from the October 2026 survey asked how long respondents are willing to endure war: 62% chose the option “as long as necessary,” a 14-point increase from April this year and the same percent as December 2025. The figure at the outset of the war in May 2022 was only 9 points higher.

We know that historical evidence does not predict the future. Nevertheless, our survey results suggest that increasing wartime hardship against Ukrainians will not coerce them into accepting territorial concessions.

articles.title: Support Global Voices’ December Spotlight: Digital Communities
paragraphs: Donate to our Digital Communities Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

Digital communications sparked new ways of forming communities: communities that spanned vast distances; that offered asynchronous interaction, innovative forms of constructing identities, and potentially enormous reach. These communities have provided connection for people who are isolated or marginalized, built powerful groups around both professional interests and unusual hobbies, and facilitated astonishing feats of knowledge-sharing and organizing, from Wikipedia to academic sub-field networks to hobby groups and fandoms.

But digital communities bring new challenges as well, from questions of moderation to questions of ownership. Almost all of them are built on the backbone of infrastructure owned by Big Tech — hardware at a minimum, usually several layers of software as well.

This is a risky place to put trust. Witness the sudden devastation when a platform is bought and sold, and what was accessible and inclusive becomes hostile; or the sudden change-to-terms-of-service maneuver, when a company leverages the trust of its users to exploit them for their sellable data. Increasingly hollowed-out echo chambers — toxic or just obliviously navel-gazing — make digital communities difficult and often dangerous to navigate. The proliferation of targeted ads, the risks of rapidly spreading mis- and disinformation, and, more recently, the insertion of large language model bots all illustrate this.

Sometimes it feels like it’s impossible to resist the tidal wave of AI slop and bot content and the all-pervasive mistrust of information engendered by the sheer amount of misinformation and disinformation we have seen produced this decade. But there are still ways to organize digitally.

The same social media that is polarizing Indian society is where young people have organized and continued to organize to resist the authoritarian Modi government. In Brazil, supporters of President Lula ran an organic, human-driven campaign that successfully beat algorithms weighted toward his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the October 2026 election. LGBTQ+ people in hostile environments often only have online spaces to find community and solidarity. People everywhere are rewilding the internet, reclaiming, reviving, and rebuilding communities everywhere in defiance of faceless, consolidated power.

In this month’s spotlight, Global Voices, in partnership with Ranking Digital Rights, will explore the multiverse of digital communities — starting with our own. We want to highlight specific communities, the tools and tactics they use to organize, resist, and overcome the algorithmic pressure from tech platforms, and show how digital communities thrive and persist the world over, defying overwhelming power asymmetries and rejecting pressure to accept the defaults.

articles.title: 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final
paragraphs: The 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final was a football match played on 18 January 2026 at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat, Morocco. It determined the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), the 35th edition of the biennial African tournament organised by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), and was contested between Senegal and hosts Morocco.

The match was marred by controversies, most notably Senegal's decision to walk off the field in protest at a disallowed goal and detrimental VAR decision in stoppage time. Senegal later returned to the pitch, and played out the match, winning 1–0 after extra time. The walk-off and subsequent fan violence were described as "unacceptable" by FIFA president Gianni Infantino, and drew legal action from the Royal Moroccan Football Federation as well as disciplinary investigations by the CAF.

On 17 March 2026, the CAF Appeal Board ruled that, when Senegal left the field and repeatedly refused to return from their dressing room, they had forfeited the game; per the rules for forfeited games, the match was deemed a 3–0 win for Morocco. The following day, the Senegalese Football Federation announced it would appeal the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. On 24 November 2026, CAS ruled in favour of Senegal, reinstating them as the winners of the tournament.

The Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium is a football stadium in Rabat, Morocco, with a seating capacity of 69,500. Opened on 5 September 2025, it is the home stadium of the Morocco national football team. It is part of a larger sports complex that includes an athletics track and field stadium, the indoor Salle Moulay Abdellah arena, and an Olympic-size swimming pool. It is one of the largest stadiums in Morocco.

CAF announced the full list of referees for the match on 18 January 2026, with referee Jean-Jacques Ndala of the Democratic Republic of the Congo being the main referee. He was assisted on the lines by Guylain Bongele Ngila and Gradel Mwanya Mbilizi, also from DR Congo. The third assistant referee (reserve) was Styven Moutsassi of the Republic of the Congo. The other officials were South African Abongile Tom as fourth referee, Pierre Atcho of Gabon as video assistant referee (VAR), and two officials as assistant video assistant referee (AVAR): Letticia Viana of Eswatini and Stephen Yiembé of Kenya.

Senegal's national football team (nicknamed "Les Lions") first burst onto the international scene when they qualified for the 2002 World Cup and defeated France in their opening match, afterwards reaching the quarterfinals. That same year they reached the AFCON final but lost to Cameroon on penalties. Senegal next qualified for the World Cup in 2018, while their performance in the 2019 AFCON where they lost 1–0 to Algeria in the final cemented their reputation as one of Africa's top sides. In 2021, propelled by Sadio Mané, Senegal won their first AFCON title by beating Egypt on penalties in the final. Prior to the 2025 AFCON, Paddy Power gave Senegal odds of 13/2 to win the tournament.

In the group stage Senegal topped Group D by goal difference, after a 3–0 win against Botswana with two goals from Nicolas Jackson, a 1–1 draw against second-placed DR Congo, and a 3–0 win against Benin despite captain Kalidou Koulibaly being shown a red card in the second half. Senegal faced Sudan in the round of 16 who they beat 3–1 after going a goal down thanks to two goals by Pape Gueye before half time. In the quarter-finals, Senegal beat Mali 1–0 due to a goal from Iliman Ndiaye and a red card for Malian midfielder Yves Bissouma. Senegal faced Egypt in the semi-finals, a rematch of the 2021 final, which pitted former Liverpool teammates Sadio Mané and Mohamed Salah against one another. Senegal largely controlled the game, with a 78th-minute goal from Mané sending them through to the final.

Morocco national football team (nicknamed the "Atlas Lions") were the tournament's hosts, and had last won the AFCON back in 1976. Their qualification for the 2018 World Cup was their first in 20 years. In the 2022 World Cup, Morocco enjoyed pan-Arab and pan-African support as they embarked on the deepest run ever made by an African team in the World Cup, beating the likes of Spain, Portugal, and Belgium on the way, before being knocked out in the semifinals and ultimately coming 4th. Prior to the 2025 AFCON, Sky Bet gave Morocco odds of 11/4 to win the tournament.

In the group stage, Morocco comfortably topped Group A following a 2–0 win against Comoros, a 1–1 draw against Mali with both goals coming from penalties, and a 3–0 win against Zambia with two goals from Ayoub El Kaabi. Brahim Díaz scored three goals throughout the group stage while key player Achraf Hakimi returned from injury towards the end. Morocco faced Tanzania in the round of 16 which ended in a 1–0 win thanks to a Díaz goal coming from a Hakimi assist. Morocco next came up against Cameroon in the quarter-finals, which saw Díaz score for a fifth game in a row in a clinical 2–0 win despite Morocco taking only three shots. Morocco faced Nigeria in the semi-finals, which proved a cagey affair as the game remained goalless after 120 minutes. In the subsequent penalty shootout goalkeeper Yassine Bounou saved two penalties to send Morocco through to the final.

The score remained level at 0–0 for most of normal time, with the match ending at a perfectly even 50–50 split in possession. The ball spent a slight majority of its time in Senegal's half, with Senegal holding possession through long defensive plays before ceding it to a Moroccan offense that repeatedly failed on short moves upfield. In the second half, Senegal dominated possession while Morocco tripled its number of shots. Moroccan goalkeeper Yassine Bounou made multiple key saves, while Senegal relied primarily on its defensive backs to keep the match goalless.

In the fifth minute of stoppage time, Senegal appeared to clinch victory from a corner kick. In the build-up to the play, Moroccan defender Achraf Hakimi was knocked to the ground while contesting the kick with Senegalese forward Abdoulaye Seck. Shortly after Hakimi fell, Seck met the incoming kick and headed it off the crossbar to set up a goal for Ismaïla Sarr. Referee Jean-Jacques Ndala made a controversial foul call against Seck, resulting in the goal being disallowed. Ndala was criticised for blowing his whistle before the play had ended, which prevented VAR from reviewing the validity of the goal.

articles.title: Why expect holiday traditions to stay the same, even as life continually changes?
paragraphs: There’s something about the holiday season that makes people notice the passage of time. As you unpack treasured decorations, prepare family recipes and listen to familiar holiday songs, you’re reminded not only of celebrations from years past but also of different times in your life.

With each passing year, children grow older, families welcome new members, relationships change, and some of those you once celebrated with are no longer here. But people often approach the holidays hoping to experience them just as they once did.

As someone who studies life transitions, I’m particularly interested in why people expect traditional holiday celebrations to remain the same when so much else in life has changed. I suggest thinking of holiday memories not as a blueprint for recreating the past but as a way to understand what makes these times meaningful to you, and how you might carry that meaning into the present.

Research on family rituals suggests that traditions contribute to a sense of identity and belonging by connecting you to the people, experiences and shared values that have shaped your life. In fact, research focused on holiday rituals has found that participating in traditions such as preparing grandmother’s chocolate fudge or watching favorite seasonal movies is associated with greater feelings of closeness and enjoyment during celebrations.

You may not recognize how tightly some holiday traditions are tied to certain stages of your life. Parents who once looked forward to Christmas morning with young children may now find themselves coordinating celebrations around the schedules of adult children and their families and in-laws. Someone who has hosted holiday gatherings for decades may find themselves adjusting to being a guest rather than orchestrating the festivities.
Although these kinds of changes are a natural part of life, they can bring a mix of emotions. You can welcome new experiences while still missing aspects of an earlier time.
During these periods of transition, the memories associated with holiday traditions may become especially meaningful, offering a connection to the past as you adjust to the present.

If you find yourself missing the holidays of years past, you may be longing not for the celebration itself but for a particular era. Memories of former times can bring comfort, but they can also evoke feelings of grief, loneliness or sadness, particularly if you’re navigating changes you didn’t anticipate or would not have chosen, such as illness, injury, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People may be more inclined to experience nostalgia, a sentimental longing for the past, during periods of transition, when familiar aspects of life are changing.
While nostalgia is sometimes viewed negatively, as dwelling on past experiences, research suggests it can be a valuable resource when navigating life changes, especially for younger generations .

For instance, nostalgia can actually strengthen social connections and contribute to a sense of meaning. Recalling cherished memories can remind you you’re part of a broader life story, which can enhance feelings of connection, personal value and purpose.
Nostalgia can also help people make sense of the different chapters of life, allowing them to maintain a sense of who they are even as circumstances change.

Memories, then, can be more than reminders of what once was. They can help you recognize what you value and inform how you experience the present. While nostalgia may not ease the pain associated with challenges such as major health changes, evolving caregiving responsibilities or military deployment, it can serve as a bridge between the past and the present.

Throughout life, people adjust routines, responsibilities and expectations to accommodate new circumstances. Yet when it comes to the holidays, they may be reluctant to make those same adjustments. Is it still Thanksgiving if the table doesn’t feature the cranberry sauce made with your family’s traditional recipe? Can it feel like Christmas if there’s no tree decorated with your family’s sentimental ornaments?

This reluctance to let holiday observances evolve may be influenced, in part, by how people remember previous celebrations. Negative emotions associated with past experiences tend to fade more quickly than positive ones . You may remember the warmth of gathering around a holiday table but less readily recall the stress or challenges that accompanied it.

When expectations no longer reflect the realities of your life, you may feel disappointed or place pressure on yourself or others to live up to those old memories. Even a cherished tradition can become a source of stress when you feel obligated to maintain it in the same way year after year.

As you navigate life’s transitions, it may be helpful to reflect on what you cherish most about your holiday traditions. Is it the way you have always celebrated? Or is it the feelings of comfort and belonging that you associate with those celebrations?
Research suggests that reflecting on the past can inspire people to seek meaningful connections and experiences in the present .

Of course, adjusting to change is not always easy, and for some, the holidays can be particularly hard . Adapting does not mean abandoning cherished traditions, directly replacing what has been lost, or feeling pressured to create new memories. It may simply mean accepting that the holidays will feel different and allowing yourself the time and space to adjust.

In the desire to recreate what once was, many people may overlook the moments that could become cherished memories in the years ahead. Savor the memories of holidays past without expecting them to define how you experience the holidays today. Celebrations don’t need to remain the same to remain meaningful.

articles.title: Immersive shopping has survived the demise of the metaverse – but its appeal depends on how it’s designed and who is using it
paragraphs: In 2021 and 2022, major retailers and fashion brands were racing into the metaverse, opening virtual stores, creating digital products and inviting consumers to explore branded worlds through avatars. Much of that excitement has since faded. But the technologies behind those experiments are far from disappearing .

Today, shoppers can try on clothes virtually, see how furniture would look in their homes and explore branded worlds on gaming platforms. Rather than building entirely new virtual universes, retailers are finding ways to integrate immersive technologies into familiar shopping experiences.

A 2025 global survey found that 53% of surveyed retail professionals focused on virtual fitting rooms, while 46% said they were building augmented reality and virtual reality experiences. On the consumer side, a 2024 survey of more than 2,200 U.S. shoppers found that 49% of respondents would buy more clothing if a great virtual try-on experience were available. Meanwhile, a separate survey found that only 4.5% of U.S. digital shoppers regularly used these technologies for shopping.
Immersive technologies continue to attract interest, but their regular use in online shopping remains limited. So what makes an immersive shopping experience worth using?

I’m a scholar of retail and consumer sciences who studies consumers’ interactions with technology in the retail environment. My research suggests that the value of immersive retail isn’t simply about how advanced or realistic the technology is. It’s about how the experience is designed, how it addresses consumers’ needs and how it helps them connect with products and brands.

Imagine shopping for a pair of sunglasses online. You like the style, but you’re not sure how they would look on you. Amazon allows shoppers to try on certain shoes and eyewear virtually using their smartphones. IKEA applies a similar concept to home furnishings through IKEA Kreativ, which allows customers to digitally remove existing furniture from their rooms and experiment with new arrangements.
These experiences address a fundamental limitation of online shopping: the gap between seeing a product on a screen and imagining how it would look on you or in your own space.

My colleagues and I found that the experience of virtually trying on clothes can be particularly helpful for shoppers who struggle to imagine how clothing would look on them. By making it easier to visualize themselves wearing a product, the technology can help them feel more comfortable with their purchase decisions. In other words, the value of immersive technology may lie less in creating a sense of novelty than in helping consumers overcome the limitations of conventional online shopping.

As artificial intelligence advances, so-called virtual try-on experiences are becoming increasingly personalized. Shoppers can now see clothing on digital representations of themselves rather than relying solely on images of fashion models. It might seem intuitive that the more closely a virtual model resembles a shopper, the better the experience. But our research suggests otherwise .

In two experiments, we found that consumers’ responses to personalized avatars depend on what psychologists call “ assessment orientation,” or the tendency to critically evaluate and compare options before making a decision. This mindset of carefully thinking through a decision can also shift depending on the shopping situation, such as choosing an outfit for a job interview versus casually browsing for fun.

Shoppers with a stronger evaluative mindset, whether due to their personal tendencies or the shopping situation, felt a stronger sense that they were the model and expressed greater intentions to buy when using personalized 3D avatars than when viewing conventional model images. Interestingly, the opposite pattern emerged among shoppers who are less inclined to mull over options.

The implication is that the same technology can offer different value to different consumers. A highly personalized experience may be particularly useful to someone who wants to thoroughly evaluate a product, but it isn’t necessarily better for everyone or every shopping situation.
Immersive technologies can also offer value beyond helping consumers decide what to buy.

Walmart, for example, has created branded experiences on Roblox, where users can explore virtual spaces, play games and discover digital products. These experiences offer retailers a new way to connect with younger consumers and build brand engagement through entertainment rather than traditional advertising. Its Walmart Discovered Roblox gaming environment has attracted nearly 40 million visits as of May 2026.

My research on branded virtual worlds suggests that simply creating a virtual space isn’t enough to engage consumers. What matters is how brands bring these spaces to life through storytelling and social experiences that help consumers feel more connected to the brand. The value of these environments lies less in their 3D graphics than in the opportunities they create for consumers to participate, interact and become part of a brand’s story.

Advances in AI will likely open up even more possibilities for immersive online shopping, from more realistic virtual try-on to interactive environments that adapt to individual preferences. But making an experience more technologically sophisticated doesn’t automatically make it more valuable.

Whether a retailer’s goal is to help shoppers visualize products, make more informed decisions or build connections with brands, they are more likely to be successful if they design experiences around consumers rather than around the capabilities of the technology.

articles.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
paragraphs: Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October.

When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands. At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea. In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year.

The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain. In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms . These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.”

Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis . Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions.

In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track. Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses.

Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas . “One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said.

In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added. “But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said.

Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season.

Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025, but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports .

Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman, following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October. The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970, according to Thoman.

Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions. The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added.

El Niño is a climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. In the Northwest Pacific, the phenomenon tends to cause storms to more readily curve northward rather than continuing westward to East Asia and Southeast Asia, some experts say, bringing more storms toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: Can Indonesian researchers ever win a Nobel? Not without overhauling the research ecosystem
paragraphs: Will Indonesia ever win the Nobel Prize? That question probably pops into some Indonesians’ minds whenever Nobel season starts in October.

The reality is that there are no shortcuts to a Nobel. Breakthroughs recognised by the committee almost always stem from foundational work done decades earlier — often when it is impossible to foresee the practical payoffs.

Take the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth for pioneering optogenetics — a breakthrough technique that uses light to control nerve cell activity.

Interestingly, the road to optogenetics began with research that seemed to have nothing to do with medicine. Hegemann was initially investigating how the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas swims towards light. His collaboration with Nagel eventually led to the discovery of channelrhodopsin — a light-sensitive protein that acts as an ion channel.

By 2005, Deisseroth’s team showed that channelrhodopsin could be harnessed to control neuronal firing with light. What began as a humble inquiry into pond algae laid the groundwork for optogenetics — now an indispensable tool for mapping and manipulating the brain.
This trajectory illustrates the road to the prestigious award: Nobel-worthy breakthroughs emerge from ecosystems patient enough to let basic research mature before demanding immediate benefits.
But can Indonesia’s research ecosystem nurture that kind of long game?
The most glaring bottleneck in Indonesia’s research ecosystem is funding. The country’s R&D spending remains low, lagging far behind its ASEAN peers.

Data from the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) paint a sobering picture: in 2024, Indonesia’s total R&D expenditure stood at around US$2.8 billion — a meagre 0.23% of gross domestic product (GDP). Higher education shouldered 71.02% of that spending, while the private sector contributed a negligible 14.96%.

Neighbours tell a different story: the private sector drove 51.37% of R&D in Malaysia (2022) and roughly 74% in Thailand (2021). The lesson is structural: a nation’s scientific muscle depends not just on how much it spends, but on who funds it.
How should public research funds be accounted for?

Researchers must naturally account for every public fund they spend: explaining what they investigate, how funds are allocated and what discoveries emerge. Yet not all grant systems in Indonesia define “results” the same way — and rigid metrics can easily distort scientific work.

Take Indonesia’s 2025 Research and Community Service Guidelines . Under the Regular Fundamental Research scheme (PFR), grantees are mandated to publish at least one paper in a reputable international journal every single year.

Research benchmarks are indeed necessary. But when success hinges on short-term milestones — like annual publication quotas — scientists are almost guaranteed to play it safe, pursuing predictable findings over ambitious, high-risk discoveries.
Take Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who jointly won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that began more than two decades earlier.

In 2005, the pair made a critical breakthrough: modifying mRNA’s nucleosides could suppress harmful inflammatory responses to synthetic mRNA. After years of funding rejections, skepticism and painstaking refinement, that fundamental discovery unlocked the mRNA vaccines and therapies that ultimately saved millions of lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.

By comparison, Japan’s Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research program, known as KAKENHI, still demands strict accountability: recipients must report on expenditure, track ongoing milestones, and submit comprehensive final evaluations.

KAKENHI explicitly urges researchers to disseminate their findings globally — via peer-reviewed journals, international partnerships, and academic conferences. Crucially, the guidelines avoid treating rigid publication targets as make-or-break funding criteria.
In 2025, China boosted its R&D spending to roughly 2.8% of GDP. Its investment in basic research surged by 13.3% year-on-year – comfortably outstripping its 8.2% overall growth in R&D expenditure.

Meanwhile, Singapore committed S$S37 billion (around US$28.77 billion) to its Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan. The blueprint balances market-driven applications with solid backing for open-ended fundamental science and homegrown scientific talent.
Both countries operate under distinct economic realities and strategic priorities. Yet they share a common thread: fundamental science remains an indispensable pillar of their national policy.

Boosting Indonesia’s research budget is crucial, but cash alone will not fix the system without deeper industry involvement and long-term backing for university laboratories. Accountability matters, too – but evaluation frameworks must be flexible enough to give unorthodox, exploratory ideas room to breathe.

After all, scientific inquiry is inherently unpredictable. Hypotheses fall flat, experiments fail and dead ends are part of the process. A project that yields no marketable innovation within five years may still unearth foundational knowledge that sparks a breakthrough decades later.

Grant systems must therefore make room for rigorous science whose outcomes cannot be mapped in advance. Such work still demands robust evaluation – just not through the same narrow, transactional metrics applied to off-the-shelf product development.

Indonesia does not need a glitzy roadmap to a Nobel Prize; it needs a dependable research ecosystem. That means reliable funding, smarter resource allocation, sensible evaluation metrics and real avenues for international collaboration.
Every nation dreams of its own Nobel laureate, and Indonesia is no exception. But the medal itself cannot be the end goal.

For Indonesia, the real debate is not a false choice between applied projects with immediate payoffs and curiosity-driven basic science. The challenge is designing an ecosystem flexible enough to nurture both, knowing full well that groundbreaking research runs on its own clock.
What matters far more is fostering a research ecosystem that empowers scientists to pursue bold, open-ended questions – even when the tangible payoffs are years or decades down the line.

articles.title: 1852 Banda Sea earthquake
paragraphs: The 1852 Banda Sea earthquake struck on 26 November at 07:40 local time, affecting coastal communities on the Banda Islands. It caused violent shaking lasting five minutes, and was assigned XI on the Modified Mercalli intensity scale in the Maluku Islands. A tsunami measuring up to 8 m (26 ft) slammed into the islands of Banda Neira, Saparua, Haruku and Ceram. The tsunami caused major damage, washing away many villages, ships and residents. At least 60 people were killed in the earthquake and tsunami. The earthquake had an estimated moment magnitude of 7.5 or 8.4–8.8, according to various academic studies.

The Banda Sea is situated in a region of complex convergence involving the Australian and Sunda plates. This complex tectonic interaction has broken the crust into a number of minor plates and microplates including the Banda Sea, Timor, Molucca Sea and Bird's Head plates. Resembling an arch, this convergent boundary is one of the most complex in the world. Oceanic lithosphere subducts to a depth greater than 600 km beneath the Banda Sea. As a consequence, the Banda Sea is a seismically active region. Many large earthquakes in the Banda Sea occur at a hypocentral depth of up to 600 km, including an Mw 7.6 which struck at 397 km (247 mi) depth. These intermediate (70–300 km (43–186 mi)) and deep-focus (>300–700 km (190–430 mi)) earthquakes are the result of dip-slip faulting within the oceanic lithosphere, which usually do not result in significant impact. The Mw 8.5–8.6 1938 Banda Sea earthquake was an intermediate-focus thrust earthquake.

At about 07:40–07:50 local time on 26 November, Banda Neira was rocked by a series of intense "vertical shocks" which developed into rolling motions. The rolling motion was directed in a northwest–southeast orientation for five minutes. The first shock was so strong that nearly every home on the island collapsed. Houses that withstood the shaking were severely cracked and became uninhabitable. Papenberg, a small peak on the island, collapsed as well. Many large cracks formed at the beaches on the island. Similar effects were described on Banda Besar. The tremors were accompanied by a loud rumble described as "cannon shots".

On the islands of Rosengain and Pulau Ai, the earthquake was also felt with a great force, later assigned XI on the Mercalli intensity scale. On Haruku Island, cracks appeared in the walls of a fort and church. Damage to structures was also reported on Saparua. The island of Ambon was undamaged but felt the tremors for five minutes intensely. On Bacan Island, trees and flagstaffs were observed swaying.

Three newly formed but small islands were seen after the earthquake. The islands were "soft and had a yellow golden color" to them. Coral remains and yellow sand was likely the composition of the islands. One of the islands later washed away while the remaining two had vegetation grown on them. Another island at 5.583°S 133.000°E﻿ / -5.583; 133.000, measuring 250 meters in diameter was also discovered.
In Surabaya, Java, weak tremors were felt, but they were likely due to a separate event.

The highest tsunami wave was recorded on the island of Banda Neira with a height of 8 meters. It struck the island approximately 25 minutes after the shaking had stopped. Many residents who witnessed the oncoming waves were frightened and fled for the hills. Sixty boat crews died when the tsunami overcame the breakwater and embankments where they had sought refuge. The waves carried with it many proas, smashing them against the embankment. Waves also wiped out buildings at the coast. Four separate waves were observed with regular intervals until 10:30 when the water began to calm down.

On Pulau Ai, the tsunami was significant, being one meter higher than the usual flood tide level. Descriptions of the tsunami in Ambon are unclear, with sources claiming the waves were 8 meters tall while others stating they were 20 cm higher than the flood tide mark. Flood damage to homes, proas and beaches occurred on Ceram Island.

Due to the lack of instrumental data, the mechanism of the earthquake is still debatable, with published sources suggesting the event was a large megathrust earthquake with an estimated moment magnitude (Mw) of 8.4 or greater. Other research journals claim it was a shallow normal faulting event with a smaller magnitude of 7.5.

A publication in 2020 led by Phil Cummins suggests the event did not occur on a megathrust fault, but rather, a shallow normal fault in the Banda Sea. The normal fault was determined as being the Banda Detachment, a shallow-dipping structure that accommodates extension of the Banda Sea. It is thought to be the only major potentially seismogenic structure to cause heavy shaking and a large tsunami. The earthquake potential and history of this structure is still poorly understood, and have never been considered a tsunami and seismic hazard to the region. The Weber Deep, a 7.2-km deep forearc basin between the megathrust front and Banda Arc volcanic chain is a massive fault scarp which formed when extension along the Banda Detachment started. However, there have been no instrumentally recorded earthquakes on this fault, therefore, it is suggested that the structure is creeping aseismically, or that earthquakes on this fault have occurred before the birth of modern seismic instruments.

The research presented a much smaller earthquake moment magnitude of only 7.5 with a rupture close to the Banda Islands. An earthquake anywhere on the megathrust is unlikely to result in violent ground motions as described in the historical accounts because it is too far from the islands. The study dismissed all reports of shaking felt in Surabaya, Java as being a separate, local earthquake which timing coincided with the one in the Banda Sea. This event in Java, named the Grati earthquake, is thought to have a magnitude of Mw 5.7–6.0 and occurred on the Pasuruan Fault.

Explicit descriptions of the tsunami in the Banda Islands described a rise in sea level, followed by a drop. This meant the earthquake could not be sourced from a subduction zone megathrust event as such a tsunami would be observed as a drawback of the water first in the same location. The Banda Islands situated on the overriding plate would experience a negative wave first before a large tsunami could hit, thus a drawback would be observed. Furthermore, a megathrust earthquake-sourced tsunami would take much longer for it to hit the islands, while historic descriptions stated that the tsunami arrived 20 minutes after the five minutes of shaking.

articles.title: Jilava massacre
paragraphs: The Jilava massacre took place during the night of 26 November 1940, at Jilava Prison, near Bucharest, Romania. Sixty-four political detainees were killed by the Iron Guard (Legion), with further high-profile assassinations in the immediate aftermath. It came about halfway through the fascist National Legionary State and led to the first open clash between the Guard and conducător Ion Antonescu, who ousted the Legion from power in January 1941.

Under King Carol II, repressive measures against the Iron Guard gathered pace in the late 1930s; a cycle of violence on both sides left many dead, including Prime Minister Armand Călinescu and Corneliu Zelea Codreanu, the Guard's founder and leader. After Carol abdicated in September 1940 and the Guard ascended to power, its members thirsted for revenge, seeking to eliminate those who had participated in the various legal and illegal actions taken by the king's regime. The more restrained Antonescu sought punishment through legal means. Within his first month in power, he approved an official probe into all those who could not account for becoming wealthy very fast in the last years of Carol's rule, and established a special court to investigate crimes committed by the previous regime's principal figures, or in their name, against the Guard.

The court ordered the arrest of those to be investigated, had them imprisoned at Jilava, and entrusted them to the custody of special Legionary formations, described by Alexandru Creţianu as "nothing less than an improvised version of the SS strong-arm squads".

The investigation underway, the court, wishing to obtain testimony from the detainees in order to prepare for their trials, ordered several of them to be transferred to another jail, where their depositions would be taken. However, Ștefan Zăvoianu, the Bucharest Prefect of Police in charge of the Legionary squads guarding the prisoners, believed Antonescu had changed his mind about executing those responsible for Codreanu's death and refused to comply with the order. This alerted the military authorities, who decided to replace the squads with regular military guards and move the prisoners themselves. Zăvoianu was informed of this decision on November 26, and that night the squads shot dead every one of their charges: politicians, senior military officers, and policemen accused of complicity in Codreanu's arrest and execution.

The 20-strong execution team, armed with semi-automatic Mauser pistols, was commanded by Dumitru Grozea, head of the Legionary Workers' Corps. Its members were aged between 18 and 25. Gheorghe Crețu, who killed 14 inmates, testified at his trial that Grozea gave the order to shoot at around 11:45 p.m., whereupon each executioner was sent to a particular cell, ordered the prisoners to stand and shot them. The executioners then gathered before the guards; together they went and paid homage before Codreanu's remains.

In all, 64 people were killed in the 19 cells of the prison. Each victim was shot at least twice; in all, some 579 bullets were fired during the 15 minutes the massacre lasted. Among those assassinated were former Prime Minister Gheorghe Argeșanu (who had presided over the reprisals following Armand Călinescu's assassination), former Justice Minister Victor Iamandi, former Bucharest police prefect and interior minister Gabriel Marinescu, several high-ranking officers of the Gendarmerie, including its head inspector General Ioan Bengliu, Colonel Zeciu (who had organised the killing of Codreanu and thirteen other Legionnaires), Majors Aristide Macoveanu and Iosif Dinulescu (who had prepared and carried out the killing), Staff Sergeant Sârbu (who had actually tightened the wire around Codreanu's neck, strangling him), as well as Mihail Vârfureanu (a former Legionnaire who turned informant and was responsible for female Guardist Nicoleta Nicolescu's assassination).

Also killed were former Chief of Secret Police Mihail Moruzov and his deputy, Niki Ștefănescu, who was shot 38 times. These two were not responsible for excesses against the Iron Guard, but in the past they paid many of its members, including Codreanu's successor as leader, Horia Sima, for services rendered as informants. Zăvoianu knew that the Legion would like to be rid of such inconvenient witnesses before any trials or investigations could take place.

As a result of the massacre, the simmering power struggle between Sima and Antonescu reached crisis proportions. Informed of what had taken place on November 27, the latter immediately called a special meeting of the Council of Ministers, demanding that the government and the Legion issue a joint public statement disassociating themselves from and condemning the recent events. When asked why they did not attempt to prevent bloodshed, the Legionary ministers denied having any foreknowledge and tried to act as surprised as anyone else. Still, they all attempted to justify the murders, claiming it was the general impression among Legionaries that the court had no intention of punishing any of the accused, whom they assumed would eventually go free. Antonescu, unswayed, declared that: "the handful of reprobates who have committed this crime will be punished in an exemplary manner. I will not allow that the country and the future of the nation be compromised by the action of a band of terrorists... I was reserving the punishment of those held at Jilava for the justice system of the country. But the street decreed otherwise, proceeding to implement justice itself".

Sima replied that such a deed would not be repeated, to which Antonescu drew his attention to the fact that Nicolae Iorga's safety was threatened by Legionaries and he should take steps to ensure no harm was done.

Sima agreed, but by the end of the day was informed that Iorga, the venerable historian and former prime minister, had been murdered. Several Guard members had attacked him and Virgil Madgearu, secretary general of the National Peasants' Party, in their homes, kidnapped and shot them, and abandoned their bodies in a roadside ditch. Also on November 27, Zăvoianu and his men rounded up more leading figures of the Carlist regime, including former prime ministers Constantin Argetoianu and Gheorghe Tătărescu (saved by the quick intervention of Lt. Col. Alexandru Rioșanu), former prime minister Ion Gigurtu (saved by Sima) and former ministers Mihail Ghelmegeanu and Nicolae Marinescu; they were brought to the Police Prefecture with the intention of executing them, but spirited away to safety in the heavily fortified building of the Interior Ministry.

articles.title: Tabancale language
paragraphs: Tabancale (Tabancal, Aconipa, Tabacanake, Tabancara) is an extinct language formerly spoken in the village of Aconipa, located along the Chinchipe River in the Department of Cajamarca, Peru, as well as in neighboring Ecuador, by the Tabancale people. Only five words were collected in the 16th century and they are not demonstrably related to those in other languages. As a result, it has been categorized as a language isolate by some and left unclassified by others; a connection has been proposed with the Chicham languages, spoken in Peru and Ecuador. The Tabancale people are thought to have switched to Quechua after they were conquered in 1549.

The surviving information about the Tabancale people and their language comes from an anonymous document titled Relación de la tierra de Jaén ('Account of the Land of Jaén'). This document was written around 1570 and published by Marcos Jiménez de la Espada as part of the Relaciones geográficas de Indias ('Geographical Accounts of the Indies') of Peru in 1887. The Relaciones were based on a series of responses by parish priests to questionnaires sent out by the Spanish royal government to survey the characteristics of the different regions of its South American territories. According to the account, the language spoken in Aconipa was different from all others. The region had been conquered for the Viceroyalty of Peru by Diego Palomino, who founded the city of Jaén de Bracamoros in 1549 at the mouth of the Chinchipe River. The anthropologists Julian Steward and Alfred Métraux believed that Tabancale speakers eventually assimilated into the rural, Quechua-speaking population after being brought into the encomienda system.

Tabancale was reported to be spoken in a single village, Aconipa, "near the upper reaches of the Chinchipe River" in Cajamarca Department near the modern-day Ecuador–Peru border, to the north of San Ignacio in Peru and south of Valladolid in Ecuador. The linguist Čestmír Loukotka put its distribution in both Peru and Ecuador.

The Tabancale spoke a "different language" from other peoples living in the region, according to the Relación. According to the linguist John Alden Mason, Loukotka was apparently the only one of the compilers of South American Indigenous languages to mention Tabancale at the time; in Loukotka's 1935 classification, he had grouped it as an independent family. The scholar Jacinto Jijón y Caamaño, in his survey of Ecuadorian Indigenous languages, only mentioned the existence of Tabancale, though he left it as "independent" in his 1943 classification. Mason himself found the data on Tabancale "insufficient to warrant its classification, at any rate as a distinct family". Loukotka and the ethnologist Paul Rivet, in their 1952 classification, grouped "Akonipa" as one of their 109 independent language families. Loukotka, in his later 1968 classification, also classified it as a language isolate, as did the linguist Antonio Tovar. According to the linguists Willem Adelaar and Pieter Muysken, the few known Tabancale vocabulary items do not show similarity with other languages; they opt to leave Tabancale unclassified for the same reason. The linguist Matthias Urban identifies a connection with the Chicham languages of Peru and Ecuador, particularly in the word yema 'water' with Chicham yumi 'water', though the linguist Alfredo Torero had previously ascribed this similarity to language contact. Urban also claims that "the remaining vocabulary does not suggest a Chicham affiliation". The linguist Lyle Campbell also considers it unclassified.
Five words of Tabancale were recorded in the Relaciones geográficas.

articles.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
paragraphs: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”
Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”
NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.
